catalog_quote: 2.1.2. Ударение падает обычно на последний слог: kōvíd ‘голубь’, kurčún ‘курица’, cəfúr ‘четыре’, potún ‘бедро’, ǰalán ‘тепло; горячий (о еде)’, awezán ‘висячий’, ... pārúzd ‘вчера’, ormózd ‘солнце’. Небольшая часть слов принимает ударение на первый слог: γóndəm ‘пшеница’, wúduγd ‘дочь’, wúznəl ‘сноха, невеста’, wúter ‘зола’, péšten ‘вымя’, dídus ‘одиннадцать’; местоимения: míčəf ‘нас’, tə́mv(el) ‘вас’, mánəf ‘этих; их’, wánəf ‘тех; их’. Морфологические показатели в основном безударны. Всегда стоят под ударением: 1) показатели мн. числа имен -ən, -ān, -āy, -ō; 2) показатель сравнительной степени -tar; 3) показатель разделительности -i; 4) личные окончания простых глагольных форм; 5) суффиксы причастий и инфинитива -ōk, -uk; 6) словообразующие суффиксы. Безударны отделяемые личные показатели. В отрицательных формах глагола главное ударение переносится на отрицание, второстепенное сохраня…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page scan we hold of Yusufbekov 2000 p.188 sec. 2.1.2 (p.189), locator correct. (2) The deciding source is a 2000 handbook grammar sketch by the language's principal modern describer, with an explicit stress paragraph; held corroboration from Morgenstierne 1938 (same initial-stress exceptions 'yondum, 'didus), Edelman & Dodykhudoeva 2009 (Pamir-wide final tendency) and Iranica on sister Ishkashimi; Beck 2012's stress-marked Sanglechi wordlist (downloaded now, open via the Internet Archive) independently shows predominantly final stress with a lexical minority of initial-stressed words. (3) The one better work, Yusufbekov & Dodykhudoeva 2008 (OIJ VII, 125 pp), is by the same author, print-only, and would at most refine the exception/morphology detail

sources.citation: Beck, Simone. 2012. The Effect of Accessibility on Language Vitality: The Ishkashimi and the Sanglechi Speech Varieties in Afghanistan. Linguistic Discovery 10(2):157-233. DOI 10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.399 (downloaded via the Internet Archive; live Dartmouth site now behind login).
sources.quote: No rule statement (sociolinguistic survey). But the 274-item wordlist transcriptions carry stress marks (ˈ as apostrophe): Sanglechi forms are predominantly final-stressed (e.g. bəˈɾɪn 'rice', dunˈba 'fat', ɪˈɡaɾ 'liver', naɾˈxukʰ 'fingernail', aˈzə 'I', əˈman 'how many') with a minority of initial-stressed items (ˈwəɾve 'barley' — cf. Ishkashimi úrvəs in Iranica — ˈɔkʰ kʰ 'egg', ˈkʰafe 'palm', ˈpaɾo). Rough tally of the Fāruq column: 82 final vs 10 non-final among stress-marked polysyllables. One variance: 'eleven' appears as diˈdus (final) in Fāruq vs Yusufbekov's dídus.
sources.locator: Appendix A: Word List Results, pp.211-219 (Sanglechi columns: Dashte Rubāt, Esketul, Fāruq); no prose stress statement anywhere in the text (a full-text search for stress/accent: only ILR-scale 'accent' on p. ~227).

sources.note: No mention of tone or pitch anywhere; the prosody content is stress only -- word stress usually final, a small set of words initial-stressed, word stress relatively weak and phrasal stress important; vowel realisations vary with presence/absence of stress; historical chapter reconstructs suffix stress in the Sanglechi-Ishkashimi stage from i-umlaut reflexes.

tone.quote: Ударение в сангличском языке обычно падает на последний слог, незначительная часть слов, принимает ударение на первый слог. Большую роль играет фразовое ударение, так как словарное ударение в сангличском как и в большинстве иранских языков относительно слабо.
tone.locator: avtoreferat, summary of Chapter I 'Fonetika', section 'Udarenie' (unpaginated; immediately before 'Struktura slova i sloga')
tone.translation: Stress in Sanglechi usually falls on the last syllable; an insignificant part of the words takes stress on the first syllable. Phrasal stress plays a large role, since word stress in Sanglechi, as in most Iranian languages, is relatively weak.

tone.quote: The accent which lies at the base of the development in Sgl.—Ishk., appears to have been of the ordinary, late Old Ir. type. ... Elision of a short vowel before the accent has taken place in krič 'hut' (< *katīčī?), possibly in cəfūr 'four', and before a secondary suffix in əṣ̌čāk 'girl' < ṣ̌əc + āk. ... The loss of the vowel in an unstressed first syllable occurs also in lw.s (e.g. Sk. bčåk 'he-goat'; bland = bɪland 'high'; brūt = bərūt 'moustache', etc.), and may be of recent date.
